subject: chemistry
title: Pure substances and melting points
key_idea: In chemistry, a pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance. A pure substance melts and boils at specific temperatures. A mixture melts over a range of temperatures, so melting point data can tell them apart.

blocks.text: This section covers the scientific meaning of pure and how it differs from everyday use.

items.meaning: A single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance.
Two or more substances together, not chemically joined.
A substance mixed in with a pure substance.

items: In everyday language, **pure** can mean nothing has been added, for example pure milk.
In chemistry, a pure substance contains only one element or compound.
Air is a mixture, because it contains several gases.
Drinking water is not pure water, because it contains dissolved ions such as calcium and sodium.
Chemistry: pure means one element or compound only.
Everyday: pure often means nothing has been added.

blocks.text: This section covers how melting and boiling points show whether a substance is pure.

items: A pure substance melts and boils at **specific temperatures**.
Its melting point is sharp: it melts at one temperature.
A mixture melts over a **range of temperatures**.
Impurities lower the melting point of a substance.
Impurities raise the boiling point of a substance.
Pure water boils at 100 °C and freezes at 0 °C.

diagram.alt: Heating curves. A pure substance stays at one temperature while it melts. A mixture keeps warming slowly while it melts over a range.

items: Mixture: melts over a range, at a lower temperature than the pure substance.

blocks.text: This section covers how to decide from data whether a sample is pure.

items.text: Look at the melting point of each sample in the table.
A single value means the sample is pure. A range of values means it is impure.
A pure sample melts at the data book value. It cannot melt above it.
Say the sample has a sharp melting point, or that it melts over a range.

diagram.alt: Sort each statement into pure substance or mixture.
diagram.prompt: Sort each statement: pure substance or mixture?

items.text: Melts gradually over a range of temperatures
Melts at a lower temperature than the data book value
Contains two or more substances mixed together

items: Look for a sharp value or a range.
A pure sample cannot melt above the pure value; impurities lower it.

checks.q: A solid melts between 78 °C and 82 °C. Is it pure? Explain.
checks.a: No. A pure substance has a sharp (specific) melting point. This solid melts over a range of temperatures.

checks.q: What does pure mean in chemistry?
checks.a: A single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance.

checks.q: Describe a test to show that a sample of water is pure.
checks.a: Boil it and check that it boils at 100 °C. Or freeze it and check that it freezes at 0 °C.

worked_example.question:
A 250 g sample of water has a boiling point of 100.60 °C. The boiling point of pure water in a data book is 100.00 °C. Each 1% of impurity increases the boiling point of water by 0.12 °C.

Calculate the mass of the impurity in the sample of water.
worked_example.tip: One mark for each step: find the percentage first, then the mass.

worked_example.question:
The melting points of three samples of S are shown in the table.

Sample | Melting point in °C
A | 160–164
B | 166
C | 163–165

State whether each of these samples, A, B and C, is pure or impure and justify your answers using the information in the table.
answer_points: B is pure; A and C are impure.
B has a sharp (single) melting point.
A and C melt over a range of temperatures, or at lower temperatures than B.
worked_example.tip: The marks are independent: you can score the reasons even if the pure or impure decisions are wrong.

worked_example.question:
A student separates two solid substances, A and B. She wants to check that they are pure.

The student measures the melting points of four samples of solid A.

Sample | Melting point (°C)
1 | 115
2 | 119
3 | 114–118
4 | 120–122

She knows that a pure sample of solid A has a melting point of 120 °C.

She concludes that sample 4 is the purest sample of solid A.

Do the results support her conclusion?

Explain your answer using evidence from the table.
answer_points: No: the results do not support her conclusion.
Pure samples do not have a range of melting points.
Sample 4 has a range that is higher than 120 °C. A pure sample cannot melt above 120 °C.
Sample 2 is likely to be the most pure.
worked_example.tip: The 'No' gets no mark by itself. Two marks are for the idea of a range or an impossible value, and one is for naming the purest sample.
